name: Fantasy Tabletop Helper
tagline: A web toolkit for tabletop RPG game masters: encounter tracking, NPC and loot generation, campaign notes.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Almost everything a GM helper does is deterministic logic over small data: roll dice, sort initiative, roll on a table, store notes. None of that needs a server, a network, or anyone else's account. The genuine work is content, well-written random tables, monster stat blocks, encounter balancing math, and open licensed material covers most of it if you are willing to paste in the SRD. Where the paid product wins is that someone already did the typing and the mobile layout works at a cramped table. Build it yourself if you run one campaign and enjoy tinkering more than you enjoy paying.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that tracks initiative and HP for an encounter, rolls dice expressions, generates NPCs and loot from editable tables, and keeps per-campaign session notes in SQLite.
requirements: Open licensed content (SRD JSON or your own tables) pasted into the seed file
A tablet or laptop you are willing to have open at the table
whatYouLose: Curated content: hundreds of hand written random tables, stat blocks and name lists you now have to source or write
A real mobile experience; your localhost app is not on your phone unless you host it
Sharing with players, so no party-facing view or shared campaign wiki
Anything the product does with licensed or system specific rules content you cannot legally copy
Someone else fixing the edge case at 9pm on game night
moatNotes: The defensible part is the library and the licensing behind it, not the initiative tracker.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because GMs are already spending their scarce prep hours on the campaign, not on building the tool that manages the campaign. Fifteen dollars a month is cheaper than a weekend, and the paid version already has the tables, the stat blocks, the mobile layout, and the muscle memory. Also, a self built tool is one more thing that can break mid session, and breaking mid session in front of five friends is a worse outcome than a subscription.
notes: The logic is trivial; the content library is the actual product, so budget your weekend for typing tables rather than writing code.
prompt:
Build a local-first tabletop RPG game master helper. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. Server actions for writes.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/gm.db, schema created on boot if missing.
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost. No auth, no external APIs.

Data model:
- campaigns (id, name, notes)
- characters (id, campaign_id, name, kind: pc|npc|monster, ac, max_hp, notes, statblock_json)
- encounters (id, campaign_id, name, round, active_index, status)
- combatants (id, encounter_id, character_id nullable, display_name, initiative, current_hp, max_hp, conditions_csv, sort_order)
- tables (id, name, entries_json) for random tables
- sessions (id, campaign_id, date, markdown)

Features, in scope:
1. Dice engine: parse and evaluate expressions like 2d6+3, 4d6kh3, 1d20+5 adv, 8d6/2. Pure function, unit tested with a seeded RNG. Inline dice roller in a persistent sidebar with a scrolling roll log.
2. Encounter runner: add combatants from the campaign roster or ad hoc, auto roll initiative, sortable list, next/prev turn with round counter, HP plus and minus with quick buttons, condition chips, concentration flag. Keyboard shortcuts: n for next turn, d to focus the dice box.
3. Random tables: CRUD editable weighted tables, roll with one click, output lands in the roll log. Seed with a handful of generic tables (tavern names, NPC quirks, minor loot, weather) written by you, plainly generic, no system specific copyrighted text.
4. NPC generator: combines name, ancestry, occupation, quirk, want, secret from tables, saves the result as an npc character in one click.
5. Session notes: markdown editor per session with autosave, rendered preview, plus a full-text search box across notes and character notes using SQLite FTS5.
6. Import: a /api/import route and a seed script that loads statblocks from a local srd.json file the user supplies; store raw JSON, render a simple stat block card.
7. Export: one button that dumps the whole DB to JSON for backup.

Out of scope, do not build: maps or battle grids, player-facing views, multiplayer sync, mobile apps, images, any bundled non-open rules content, login.

Deliverables: working app, seed script, README with setup, and vitest tests for the dice parser and initiative ordering. Put nothing in .env because there are no secrets; if you add any later, read them from .env and commit .env.example only.
